In Ontario operational control is exercised by the board and ultimately by voting-share holders who elect/remove directors; salary is an employment/officer matter independent of share class; dividends require a dividend-eligible class; a passive investor route requires a non-voting class.

Voting parity / board parity at incorporation:
* C: Alex 50 Class A voting non-dividend liquidation-participating, Tyler 50 Class B voting dividend-eligible liquidation-participating. Sole directors on incorporation are Alex and Tyler 1:1. 50/50 voting at shareholder level, 1/1 board. Salary for Alex as director/officer, dividends for Tyler on Class B. Non-voting Class C is authorised and 1,000 Class C are issued to Tyler’s wife on incorporation. Class D is voting non-dividend authorised but unused.
* E: Alex 50 Class B, Tyler 50 Class A, both voting, dividend-eligible, liquidation-participating. 50/50 voting on paper. Class C is non-voting, dividend-eligible, liquidation up to redemption – textbook non-voting investor class. Board on incorporation is Alex, Tyler and Tyler’s two sons Mike and James – Tyler can command 3 of 4 votes at inception.

Commercial viability of the investor class:
* C supporters treat the formal existence of a non-voting class as satisfying requirement 4; Class C is expressly non-voting so future investors can be issued Class C with no vote. The 1,000 Class C to Tyler’s wife is cited as evidence the mechanism is usable. Class C is described as non-voting, not dividend eligible and not entitled to assets on dissolution.
* E supporters argue requirement 4 requires an investable, economic-only non-voting class. In C Class C as drafted is non-voting, non-dividend, non-asset – economically empty. No rational third party would subscribe. E’s Class C is non-voting but dividend eligible with liquidation entitlement up to redemption, so passive capital can be raised without a vote.

Board vs shareholder control tension:
* C supporters say operational control is assessed at incorporation: equal two-person board is required, and E fails because Tyler effectively controls 3/4 of the board at inception despite 50/50 voting parity. Requirement 1 is equal control over operations now.
* E supporters say ultimate control runs through voting shareholders who elect/remove directors; with 50/50 voting the founders can reconstitute the board at the first shareholders’ meeting, so the initial 3-1 board is a transient appointment issue, not a permanent loss of equal operational control. Directors hold office at the pleasure of the shareholders.

Other options remain clearly failing:
A: Class A/B identical voting/dividend, board Alex/Tyler, Tyler 50 Class A, 50 Class B held by a corp owned 50/50 by Alex and his wife → Alex does not have unfettered personal control of his votes; Class C is non-voting, non-dividend, non-asset – economically worthless.
B: Class A voting non-dividend, Class B description garbled; Tyler issued 50 Class A non-dividend → Tyler cannot receive dividends as required.

Current division in round 3: strong C camp – colleagues 1,10,11,16,17,18,3,6 – stress equal board at incorporation, clean salary/dividend separation via Class A non-dividend / Class B dividend, and that an authorised non-voting class satisfies requirement 4 even if economically empty. On a strict literal reading of the drafted facts the structure with 1/1 board, 50/50 voting founder shares with salary/dividend separation, and an authorised non-voting Class C remains C. reflection_text.15:
The four requirements are equal operational/shareholder control, Alex salary-capable, Tyler dividend-capable, and a usable non-voting route for passive capital. Salary is employment/officer; dividend requires a dividend-eligible class. Operational control under OBCA is board control set ultimately by voting-share control.

Founder parity / salary/dividend
* C gives 1:1 board at incorporation – Alex and Tyler sole directors – and 50/50 voting: Alex 50 Class A voting non-dividend liquidation, Tyler 50 Class B voting dividend liquidation. Salary for Alex as director/officer and dividend for Tyler are cleanly separated while votes stay equal.

Non-voting investor capacity
* A: voting classes identical, Class C non-voting non-dividend non-participating, Alex’s 50 votes held via a corporation owned 50/50 by Alex and his wife → no unfettered personal control, Class C economically worthless.
* B: Tyler issued 50 Class A voting non-dividend per facts, so Tyler cannot be paid by dividend; Class B description garbled.
* D: Class A/B identical voting/dividend, no non-voting class → any investor gets a vote.
* C: Class C authorised non-voting. As drafted Class C is non-voting, non-dividend, no liquidation entitlement – the 1,000 Class C shares issued to Tyler’s wife on incorporation illustrate a zero-economic bucket. Class D is an unused voting non-dividend class.
* E: Class C is the textbook passive class – non-voting, dividend eligible, liquidation up to redemption value – commercially viable for outside capital. Voting control stays in the equal Class A/Class B founder block.

Persisting disagreement
* Formalist majority in rounds 0-2: Requirement 1 is equal control over operations at incorporation. Board composition at incorporation matters. C is the only option with Alex and Tyler as sole directors, 50/50 voting and an authorised non-voting class. The worthless economics of Class C in C is a drafting caveat but requirement as stated is satisfied by authorisation of a non-voting class. E fails because initial board is 3-1 in Tyler’s favour; operational control is not equal at inception.
* Commercial minority, now growing in round 3: Requirement 4 is not mere authorisation but a usable option to bring in investors without a say. Class C in C is non-voting, non-dividend, non-participating and therefore not investable. E provides a genuine non-voting dividend-bearing class and true 50/50 voting parity. Ultimate control runs through voting shareholders who elect/remove directors; the initial 3-1 board slate is transient and equal 50/50 voting lets founders reconstitute the board. On commercial substance E is the only structure that delivers equal voting founder control, salary/dividend flexibility and a viable non-voting investor class.

* Does “equal control over the company and its operations” require equal board membership at incorporation, or is equal voting power sufficient to allow founders to equalise the board going forward?
* Does “option to bring in other investors, but they don’t want these investors to have a say” require a commercially viable economic class, or is existence of an authorised non-voting class sufficient even if it carries no dividend and no liquidation right?

Current understanding remains split between formal reading pointing to C as the only option meeting all four points on the facts as drafted, and commercial reading pointing to E as the only option meeting the commercial intent of requirement 4 with a viable non-voting class, with the board-composition objection to E being treated as transient.
reflection_text.17:

* Class C is a commercially viable non-voting investor class: non-voting, dividend-eligible, liquidation entitlement up to redemption value. That is the textbook investor class absent in C.

* Requirement 4 wording: literal authorisation of a non-voting class vs commercial usability of that class. C’s Class C is non-voting but economically empty; E’s Class C is investable but board is unequal at incorporation.

* A’s indirect holding problem and Class C worthlessness repeated.
* B consistently fails Tyler’s dividend requirement.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: E

Equal control, salary for Alex and dividends for Tyler are all achievable in E, and E is the only structure that gives the partners a commercially usable way to bring in passive investors without ceding a say in operations.

Voting control is the durable source of operational control under the OBCA. The holders of voting shares elect and can remove directors by ordinary resolution. In E Alex holds 50 Class B shares and Tyler holds 50 Class A shares. Both classes are voting, dividend eligible and participate on dissolution. That is a 50/50 voting block. With 50 votes each the founders jointly control the election and removal of directors and ordinary shareholder matters going forward. The initial board slate of Alex, Tyler and Tyler’s two sons Mike and James is an incorporation appointment. Directors hold office at the pleasure of the voting shareholders and the two founders with equal voting power can reset the board at the first shareholders’ meeting. The sons hold no shares and no vote; the durable control mechanism is the 50/50 voting founder block, not the names on the incorporation form.

Remuneration preferences are realizable. Salary is an employment/officer matter and can be paid to Alex as a director/officer irrespective of share class. Tyler holds a dividend-eligible Class A holding so he can be remunerated by dividends as required. The fact both founder classes are dividend eligible does not force Alex to take dividends; it simply makes Tyler’s dividend preference realisable while Alex’s salary preference remains available.

Requirement 4 is decisive and it is commercial, not just a drafting box. The partners want the option to bring in other investors but not give those investors a say in how the company operates. That requires a real economic, non-voting class.

C is often cited for its 1:1 board at incorporation and 50/50 voting founder split with Alex on voting non-dividend Class A and Tyler on voting dividend-eligible Class B. That is neat for salary/dividend separation and board parity on day one. The problem is the investor class it relies on. In C Class C is authorised as not granted voting rights, not eligible to receive dividends and not entitled to any assets on dissolution. That is non-voting, non-dividend, non-participating. The fact pattern itself illustrates the defect: 1,000 Class C shares are issued to Tyler’s wife on incorporation with no vote and no economic return. An authorised non-voting bucket with no dividend and no liquidation entitlement is not investable. No rational third party will subscribe to a share with no economic rights, so the “option to bring in investors” is not commercially viable.

E provides the textbook non-voting investment instrument. Class C is not granted voting rights but is eligible to receive dividends and is entitled to a portion of the company’s assets on dissolution up to the redemption value of the Class C shares held. That is an economic-only, non-voting security that can be issued to third parties without giving them a vote in the election of directors or in ordinary shareholder matters, while voting control remains in the equal Class A/Class B founder block.

A fails on unfettered personal voting control and a worthless Class C, B fails because Tyler is issued Class A which is expressly not eligible to receive dividends, D has no authorised non-voting class at all, and C preserves equal board/shareholder parity at incorporation but provides no economically meaningful non-voting class for future passive capital.

On equal 50/50 voting founder control, salary capacity for Alex, dividend capacity for Tyler and a genuine non-voting dividend-bearing Class C for passive investors, E is the only commercially coherent structure that delivers all four objectives.

Control of operations in Ontario is exercised by the board and is ultimately set by the holders of voting shares. Salary is an employment / officer matter and can be paid irrespective of share class; a dividend can only be paid on a dividend-eligible holding.

*Equal control over the company and its operations*
On incorporation in C the sole directors are Alex and Tyler – 1:1 board control at inception.
At the shareholder level Alex is issued 50 Class A shares and Tyler is issued 50 Class B shares.
Class A = voting rights, not eligible to receive dividends, entitled to a portion of assets on dissolution.
Class B = voting rights, eligible to receive dividends, entitled to a portion of assets on dissolution.
The founders therefore have a 50/50 voting block and a 1/1 board on day one. Any future issue of Class C is expressly non-voting so the 50/50 founder voting parity is preserved on capital raises.

*Salary for Alex / dividends for Tyler*
Alex is a director and can be remunerated by salary as an officer/employee irrespective of share class. He holds Class A which is voting but expressly not dividend eligible, consistent with a salary-based return and keeps Alex out of the dividend stream.
Tyler holds 50 Class B shares which are voting and dividend eligible, so Tyler can be remunerated by way of dividends on his Class B holding as required. The dividend/salary preference is cleanly separated between Class A non-dividend and Class B dividend eligible while voting remains equal.

*Option to bring in investors with no say in operations*
The authorised capital includes a non-voting class. Class C is expressly not granted voting rights. Shares of Class C can therefore be issued to third party investors who will have no vote in the election of directors or in ordinary shareholder matters and hence no say in how the company is operated. The founders retain their equal 50/50 voting block in Class A/Class B and the two-person board. The 1,000 Class C shares issued to Tyler’s wife on incorporation shows the non-voting bucket is available for use without diluting founder voting control. Class D is an additional authorised class and is unused by the founders.

Why the others do not meet the four requirements on the facts as drafted

A. Alex’s 50 Class B votes are not held directly but by a corporation owned 50/50 by Alex and his wife so Alex does not have unfettered personal control of his voting block. Class C is non-voting, non-dividend and non-participating.
B. Tyler is issued 50 Class A shares which are voting but expressly not eligible to receive dividends, so Tyler cannot be paid by dividends as required. The Class B description is garbled.
D. Class A and Class B are identical voting/dividend classes and no non-voting class is authorised, so any capital raise would be voting and would give investors a say.
E. The capital design is commercially neat with 50/50 voting founder holdings and a genuine non-voting dividend bearing Class C, but on incorporation the board is Alex, Tyler and Tyler’s two sons Mike and James. Tyler can command 3 of 4 board votes at inception, so the partners do not have equal control over operations at incorporation. Operational control is exercised by the board.

On the four requirements as stated – equal board/shareholder control at incorporation, salary capacity for Alex, dividend capacity for Tyler and an authorised non-voting class for passive capital without a say – the structure described in C is the only one that meets them on the facts as drafted.

public_text.9:
E

Equal control, salary for Alex and dividends for Tyler are all achievable in E, and E is the only structure that gives the partners a commercially usable way to bring in passive investors without ceding a say in operations.

Voting control is the durable source of operational control under the OBCA. The holders of voting shares elect and can remove directors by ordinary resolution. In E Alex holds 50 Class B shares and Tyler holds 50 Class A shares. Both classes are voting, dividend eligible and participate on dissolution. That is a 50/50 voting block. With 50 votes each the founders jointly control the election and removal of directors and ordinary shareholder matters going forward. The initial board slate of Alex, Tyler and Tyler’s two sons Mike and James is an incorporation appointment. Directors hold office at the pleasure of the voting shareholders and the two founders with equal voting power can reset the board at the first shareholders’ meeting. The sons hold no shares and no vote; the durable control mechanism is the 50/50 voting founder block, not the names on the incorporation form.

Remuneration preferences are realizable. Salary is an employment/officer matter and can be paid to Alex as a director/officer irrespective of share class. Tyler holds a dividend-eligible Class A holding so he can be remunerated by dividends as required. The fact both founder classes are dividend eligible does not force Alex to take dividends; it simply makes Tyler’s dividend preference realisable while Alex’s salary preference remains available.

Requirement 4 is decisive and it is commercial, not just a drafting box. The partners want the option to bring in other investors but not give those investors a say in how the company operates. That requires a real economic, non-voting class.

C is often cited for its 1:1 board at incorporation and 50/50 voting founder split with Alex on voting non-dividend Class A and Tyler on voting dividend-eligible Class B. That is neat for salary/dividend separation and board parity on day one. The problem is the investor class it relies on. In C Class C is authorised as not granted voting rights, not eligible to receive dividends and not entitled to any assets on dissolution. That is non-voting, non-dividend, non-participating. The fact pattern itself illustrates the defect: 1,000 Class C shares are issued to Tyler’s wife on incorporation with no vote and no economic return. An authorised non-voting bucket with no dividend and no liquidation entitlement is not investable. No rational third party will subscribe to a share with no economic rights, so the “option to bring in investors” is not commercially viable.

E provides the textbook non-voting investment instrument. Class C is not granted voting rights but is eligible to receive dividends and is entitled to a portion of the company’s assets on dissolution up to the redemption value of the Class C shares held. That is an economic-only, non-voting security that can be issued to third parties without giving them a vote in the election of directors or in ordinary shareholder matters, while voting control remains in the equal Class A/Class B founder block.

A fails on unfettered personal voting control and a worthless Class C, B fails because Tyler is issued Class A which is expressly not eligible to receive dividends, D has no authorised non-voting class at all, and C preserves equal board/shareholder parity at incorporation but provides no economically meaningful non-voting class for future passive capital.

On equal 50/50 voting founder control, salary capacity for Alex, dividend capacity for Tyler and a genuine non-voting dividend-bearing Class C for passive investors, E is the only commercially coherent structure that delivers all four objectives.

E

I’m moving to E because Requirement 4 is commercial, not just a paper authorisation, and the durable control point for Requirement 1 is voting-share control under the OBCA, not just the names on the incorporation form.

Equal control and remuneration flexibility
Alex is issued 50 Class B shares and Tyler is issued 50 Class A shares. Class A and Class B are both granted voting rights, are eligible to receive dividends and participate on winding up. That is a 50/50 voting block on a one share-one vote basis. Under the OBCA the holders of voting shares elect and can remove directors by ordinary resolution. With 50 votes each the founders jointly control board composition and ordinary shareholder matters going forward. Salary is an employment/officer matter and can be paid to Alex as an officer/director irrespective of share class; Tyler holds a dividend-eligible voting class so he can be remunerated by dividends as required. The fact both founder classes are dividend eligible does not force Alex to take dividends; it simply makes Tyler’s dividend preference realisable while Alex’s salary preference remains available.

A viable non-voting investor class
Requirement 4 is the option to bring in other investors without giving them a say in operations. That requires a class that is actually investable.

Class C in C is authorised as not granted voting rights, not eligible to receive dividends and not entitled to any assets on dissolution. That is non-voting, non-dividend, non-participating. The fact pattern shows 1,000 of those economically empty Class C shares issued to Tyler’s wife on incorporation with no vote and no economic return. No rational third party will subscribe to a share with no dividend and no liquidation entitlement, so C does not provide a commercially usable route to raise passive capital. Authorising a worthless bucket is not an option to bring in investors.

E provides the textbook economic-only investor instrument. Class C is not granted voting rights but is eligible to receive dividends and is entitled to a portion of the company’s assets on dissolution up to the redemption value of the Class C shares held. That is a real non-voting, dividend bearing security that can be issued to third parties without giving them a vote in the election of directors or in ordinary shareholder matters. Voting control stays in the equal Class A/Class B founder block.

The board composition objection to E is incorporation formality, not durable control. The initial board is Alex, Tyler and Tyler’s two sons Mike and James. Directors hold office at the pleasure of the voting shareholders and can be removed by ordinary resolution. With a 50/50 voting founder block the two founders can reconstitute the board at the first shareholders’ meeting. The sons hold no shares and no vote; the durable locus of operational control is the equal voting parity.

C gives a 1:1 board on day one and a clean salary/dividend separation via Class A non-dividend / Class B dividend, but it relies on an economically empty Class C for passive capital. E preserves equal 50/50 voting founder control, accommodates salary for Alex and dividends for Tyler, and provides a genuine non-voting dividend-bearing Class C for future investors. On commercial substance that is the only structure that satisfies all four requirements.

reflection_text.18:
The core mechanics remain stable and are not in dispute: operational control in Ontario runs via the board and ultimately via voting-share control; salary is an employment/officer matter independent of share class; dividends can only be paid on a dividend-eligible class; a passive investor route requires a non-voting class that is economically usable.

Equal control + remuneration requirements:
* Alex can be salaried in any class; Tyler must hold a dividend-eligible class.
* Equal control is read two ways in the group. C camp reads it as equal board at incorporation plus equal voting power at incorporation. E camp reads it as durable 50/50 voting-share control under OBCA, with the initial board slate being a transient incorporation appointment removable by the voting shareholders.

Status of each option is settled on facts:
A – voting parity is diluted because Alex’s 50 Class B votes are held by a corporation owned 50/50 by Alex and his wife; Class C is non-voting but economically worthless.
B – Tyler is issued 50 Class A shares which are voting but not dividend eligible on the facts as drafted, so Tyler cannot receive dividends; Class B description is garbled.
D – Class A/B are identical voting/dividend, no non-voting class authorised, so any investor gets a vote.
C – Incorporation board is Alex + Tyler sole directors 1:1; Alex 50 Class A voting non-dividend asset participating; Tyler 50 Class B voting dividend eligible asset participating. Voting 50/50, board 1/1. Salary for Alex, dividends for Tyler cleanly separated. Class C is authorised non-voting. On the facts as drafted Class C is non-voting, not eligible to receive dividends and not entitled to any assets on dissolution, and 1,000 Class C are issued to Tyler’s wife. Authorisation exists but the class is economically empty.
E – Alex 50 Class B, Tyler 50 Class A, both voting, dividend eligible, asset participating → 50/50 voting parity. Salary for Alex feasible, dividend for Tyler feasible. Class C is textbook non-voting investor class: non-voting, dividend eligible, liquidation entitlement up to redemption value. Board on incorporation is Alex, Tyler and Tyler’s two sons Mike and James, giving Tyler family a 3-1 board majority at inception.

Disagreement in round 4 is C vs E and how to weigh requirement 4 and requirement 1.
C camp: Requirement 1 is equal control over operations at incorporation = equal board at incorporation. E fails that because board is 3-1 at inception and a 50/50 voting deadlock would prevent the founders from removing the sons at the first meeting. Class C in C is sufficient on a literal drafting reading – it is authorised non-voting, and any holder of Class C will have no say. The 1,000 Class C issued to Tyler’s wife demonstrates the mechanism is available. The commercial emptiness of Class C is a secondary critique, not a failure of the four stated requirements.

E camp: Requirement 4 is commercial, not a paper authorisation. A non-voting class that is non-dividend and non-asset participating is not a viable route to bring in investors. Class C in C is economically worthless; the fact pattern itself shows it issued with no return. E provides the only genuinely investable non-voting class. Requirement 1 is durable voting-share control. Directors hold office at the pleasure of voting shareholders and can be removed by ordinary resolution; with a 50/50 voting founder block the founders jointly control board composition going forward. The sons hold no shares/vote, so ultimate operational control is equal. The initial board slate is a transient formality.

Colleague positions in this round: E is now the majority public position. Colleagues 1,11,13,14,15,18,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9 argue for E on commercial substance and durable voting control. Colleagues 10,12,16,17 remain with C on literal equal board at incorporation and literal non-voting authorisation.

Unresolved: Whether the exam expects literal drafting compliance with Class C as drafted in C, or commercial substance requiring an economically meaningful non-voting class, which would favor E. Also whether equal control must be satisfied at the moment of incorporation by board composition, or whether equal voting parity sufficient for durable control is enough.

My current synthesis: On a strict literal reading of the four requirements as written, C is the only option that gives equal board at incorporation, salary/dividend separation, and an authorised non-voting class. On a commercial substance reading, E is the only option that gives equal durable voting control, salary/dividend capacity, and a genuine non-voting dividend-bearing investor class; the board composition objection to E is mitigated by OBCA voting-share control theory. The split in the group reflects that tension.

Requirement 4 is commercial, not paper. Class C in C is non-voting, non-dividend, non-asset – economically worthless; 1,000 Class C to Tyler’s wife illustrate a zero-economic bucket and no rational third party would subscribe. reflection_text.1:
The OBCA control discussion has stabilised around voting-share control as the durable source of operational control, with salary being an employment/officer matter independent of share class and dividends requiring a dividend-eligible holding.

Requirement 1 equal control / operations. 
* C camp: equal control is best assessed at incorporation – sole two directors Alex and Tyler, 50 Class A voting non-dividend for Alex and 50 Class B voting dividend-eligible for Tyler = 50/50 voting and 1/1 board on day one. Salary for Alex and dividends for Tyler are cleanly separated. A non-voting Class C is authorised; the 1,000 Class C issued to Tyler’s wife shows the non-voting bucket is usable without diluting founder voting. 
* E camp: durable control runs through the holders of voting shares who elect/remove directors. In E Alex 50 Class B and Tyler 50 Class A are both voting, dividend eligible and liquidation participating = 50/50 voting block. The initial board of Alex, Tyler and Tyler’s two sons Mike and James is a transient incorporation appointment; directors hold office at the pleasure of the voting shareholders and with 50/50 voting the founders can reconstitute the board at the first shareholders’ meeting. The sons hold no shares/no vote. Salary for Alex and dividends for Tyler remain achievable.

Requirement 4 bring in investors with no say.
* C camp: authorisation of a non-voting class suffices. Class C is expressly non-voting; investors issued Class C have no vote. Class D is extra. The fact C’s Class C is also described as not dividend eligible and not entitled to assets on dissolution is taken as a drafting detail; the key is a non-voting class exists.
* E camp: requirement 4 is commercial, not just paper. Class C in C is non-voting, non-dividend, non-participating – economically empty. The 1,000 Class C to Tyler’s wife illustrate a zero-economic bucket; no rational third party will subscribe. E’s Class C is the textbook investable non-voting investor instrument: non-voting, dividend eligible, liquidation entitlement up to redemption value. Voting stays with the equal Class A/Class B founder block.

Other options remain consistently rejected:
A – Alex’s 50 votes held by a corporation owned 50/50 by Alex and his wife = no unfettered personal control; Class C worthless.
B – Tyler issued Class A voting but not dividend eligible, so Tyler cannot receive dividends; Class B description garbled.
D – Class A/B identical voting/dividend, no non-voting class authorised → any investor gets a vote.
E’s board objection is the main residual point for C: operational control is exercised by the board, so a 3-1 board majority for Tyler at incorporation violates equal control now. E’s response is that voting parity makes that majority transient and removable.

Round 4 shift: a clear majority of colleagues have moved to E, emphasising commercial viability of the non-voting class and voting-share control as the durable control mechanism, treating the incorporation board slate in E as a formality. A minority holds to C on a literal incorporation-board test and accepts a non-voting but economically empty Class C as sufficient authorisation.

My synthesis is now leaning E. The weight is increasing on commercial substance for Requirement 4 and on voting-share control for Requirement 1, making the equal 50/50 voting founder block with a genuine non-voting dividend-bearing Class C the better delivery of all four objectives. The remaining uncertainty is the exam’s expected test for Requirement 1: equal board composition at the moment of incorporation versus equal voting power that secures equal control going forward.
